newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israel, PLO differ over future West Bank pullbacks.
newsitem.headline: Israel, PLO differ over future West Bank pullbacks.

text.p: Less than 48 hours after Israel and the PLO clinched a deal on Hebron, the sides differed on Thursday on how additional Israeli pullbacks in the West Bank would be decided.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu insisted a U.S. letter of guarantees stated Israel alone would define the scope of three further withdrawals from rural West Bank lands slated to follow the handover of most of Hebron to the Palestinians.
The PLO said it understood the depth of the pullbacks would be jointly determined.

Under U.S. documents accompanying the Hebron deal sealed on Wednesday, the rural withdrawals agreed by Israel in a 1995 interim self-rule accord are due to start in March and be completed by mid-1998.
"Israel will be the one that will determine the nature and scope of the three redeployments - not just the first and second one, but also the third," Netanyahu told parliament.
"This is also how the United States interprets the agreements," he added.
But the PLO insisted the size of "specified military locations" to which Israeli troops in the West Bank are to withdraw is a matter for negotiation.
While both sides gave differing interpretations, one thing was clear: the issue would continue to cloud the future of Israel-PLO peace steps.

"It is our understanding that the determination of the military locations will be carried out by the two sides and not by Israel alone," chief PLO negotiator Saeb Erekat said in a letter he sent to U.S. peace mediator Dennis Ross on Thursday.
But the U.S. State Department confirmed on Wednesday Israel would define the depth of the future pullbacks.

"The letters of assurance...refers to the process of further redeployments as an Israeli responsibility, which includes its (Israel) designating specified military locations," spokesman Nicholas Burns said in a statement issued in Washington.

Also, a "note for the record, prepared by the United States at the request of the parties, makes clear that further redeployment phases are issues for implementation by Israel rather than issues for negotiation with the Palestinians," Burns added.
